# Introduction

Our analysis is on water potability dataset. Our scope is to classify each registered water as potable or not depending on its chemical properties. The datasate can be downloaded from this site: \url{https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uom190346a/water-quality-and-potability}.

```{r setup, , echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(naniar)
library(visdat)
library(moments)
library(corrplot)
library(caret)
library(boot)
library(MASS)
library(ROCR)
library(tree)
library(randomForest)
library(gbm)
```

# Description fo the dataset

We first analyse our dataset.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}

cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

Water <-read.csv("C:/Users/Andrea/Desktop/Supervised analysis/water_potability.csv",
                  header = TRUE)
str(Water)

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n")
```

There are 10 variables. In particular:

-   9 variables are represented by real number:

    -   \textbf{ph}: The ph level fo the water.
    -   \textbf{Hardnes}: A measure of mineral content.
    -   \textbf{Solids}: Total dissolved solids in the water.
    -   \textbf{Chloramines}: Chloramines concentration in the water.
    -   \textbf{Sulfate}: Sulfate concentration in the water.
    -   \textbf{Conductivity}: Electrical conductivity of the water.
    -   \textbf{Organic carbon}: Organic carbon content in the water.
    -   \textbf{Trihalomethanes}: Trihalomethanes concentration in the water.
    -   \textbf{Turbidity}: Turbidity level, a measure of water clarity.

-   1 integer variable \textbf{Potability} that can be 0 or 1 to represent respectively not potable and potable.

# Missing values

Now we analyse missing values in our dataset.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")
miss_var_summary(Water)
cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n")

```

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
vis_dat(Water)
vis_miss(Water)
```

From the graphs we can notice that only three of the original variables are missing. The first table shows the number of missing values and its percentage. The second and the third graph shows which value is missing. Note that the 4.4% refers to the total number of missing values across all measurements for all variables.

To better understand the distribution of the data across each class, we analyse only NA for each variable depending on the potability.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
Water.NotP <- subset(Water,Potability == 0)
Miss.NotP <- miss_var_summary(Water.NotP)
Water.P <- subset(Water,Potability == 1)
Miss.P <- miss_var_summary(Water.P)

cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")
for (i in 1:nrow(Miss.NotP)){
  if(Miss.NotP$n_miss[i] > 0){
    Sulfate.NotP <- Miss.NotP$n_miss[i]
    cat("Percentage of missing values for ph in Not Potable water: ",
        Sulfate.NotP/nrow(Water.NotP)*100,"\n")

    Sulfate.P <- Miss.P$n_miss[i]
    cat("Percentage of missing values for ph in Potable water: ",
        Sulfate.P/nrow(Water.P)*100,"\n","-------------------------------------------","\n")
  }
}
cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n")
```
The percentage is calculated over the number of rows related to each class. The result highlights the possibility of MCAR.



We need to understand the number of rows that have at least one NA value.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")
# Number of rows
n_tot <- nrow(Water)

# Number of rows with NA
n_complete <- sum(complete.cases(Water))

# Number of rows that will be eliminated
n_lose <- sum(!complete.cases(Water))

cat("Total number of rows:", n_tot, "\n")
cat("Remaining number of rows without NA:", n_complete, "\n")
cat("Number of rows with NA:", n_lose, "\n")
cat("Percentage of rows with NA values:",round(n_lose/n_tot*100,2),"%")

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```

We cannot delete all these rows from our analysis, it would affect our statistical result. So I decided to substitute to NA value the respective median for that variable.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
Water.clear <- Water

# For cycle for each column
for(col in names(Water.clear)) {
  # Checking if the variable is numeric or not
  if(is.numeric(Water.clear[[col]])) {
    # Deriving the median, but removing the NA values from our calcolous
    median_col <- median(Water.clear[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
    # Substituting the values
    Water.clear[[col]][is.na(Water.clear[[col]])] <- median_col
  }
  else{
    Water.clear[[col]] <- Water[[col]] 
  }
}
```

\section{Univariate analysis}

First of all we analyse our potability variable.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}

cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

# Changing 0-1 in Not Potable-Potable
Water.clear$Potability <- factor(Water.clear$Potability, levels = c(0, 1), 
                                 labels = c("Not Potable", "Potable"))

# Deriving the total number of Not Potable - Potable
counts <- table(Water.clear$Potability)
percentage <- prop.table(counts) * 100

# Resume table
tab <- data.frame(
  Category = names(counts),
  Frequency = as.numeric(counts),
  Relative_frequecy = paste0(round(as.numeric(percentage), 2), "%")
)

print(tab)

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
# Deriving the top value for the y axis
max_y <- max(counts) * 1.2

# Creation of the barplot
barplot(
  counts,
  main = "Bar plot of Potability",
  xlab = "Potability",
  ylab = "Counts",
  col = c("coral", "lightgreen"),
  ylim = c(0, max_y)
)
# Adding the grid
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, lty = 2, col = "gray80")

# For a clear representation we plot again

barplot(
  counts,
  col = c("steelblue", "#E06D53"),
  ylim = c(0, max_y),
  add = TRUE
)

```

## Potable or Not Potable for each variable

Now we will analyse the incidence of potability for each variable. It's represented by the boxplot comparing Potable case vs Not Potable case and then adding histograms of these two cases and their summary.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
# Taking only names of variables that do not correspond to Potability
cols <- setdiff(names(Water.clear), "Potability")


# Cycle for creating all boxplots
for (col in cols) {
  # Creating the row of graphs
  par(mfrow= c(1,3), oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0))
  
  # Creating the boxplot
  boxplot(
    Water.clear[[col]] ~ Water.clear$Potability,
    main = col,
    xlab = "Potability",
    ylab = "Values",
    col = c("#E06D53", "steelblue")
  )
  grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, lty = 2, col = "gray80")
  # Adding the box to the graph
  box(which = "figure", col = "gray50", lwd = 1.5)
  
  # Save the variable if Potable or Not Potable
  NPot <- Water.clear[[col]][Water.clear$Potability == "Not Potable"]
  Pot <- Water.clear[[col]][Water.clear$Potability == "Potable"]
  
  # Creating the histogram for Not Potable
  hist( NPot,
        breaks = "FD", 
        main = paste("Histogram of ",col,"\n if Not Potable"),
        col = "#E06D53",
        border = "white",
        xlab = col,
        freq = TRUE)
  grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, lty = 2, col = "gray80")
  box(which = "figure", col = "gray50", lwd = 1.5)
  
  # Creating the histogram for Potable
  hist( Pot,
        breaks = "FD", 
        main = paste("Histogram of ",col,"\n if Potable"),
        col = "steelblue",
        border = "white",
        xlab = col,
        freq = TRUE)
  grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, lty = 2, col = "gray80")
  box(which = "figure", col = "gray50", lwd = 1.5)
  
  # Title for the line of graphs
  mtext(col, 
      side = 3,         
      outer = TRUE,     
      cex = 1.4,        
      font = 2,         
      line = 1)  
  
  # Summary if Not Potable variable
  cat(paste("Summary of ", col , " if Not Potable\n"))
  cat("\n")
  print(summary(NPot))
  V<- var(NPot)
  cat("Variance : ",V,"\n")
  Sd <- sd(NPot)
  cat("Standard deviation : ",Sd,"\n")
  NPot.table <- table(NPot)
  mode <- names(NPot.table)[which.max(NPot.table)]
  cat("Mode : ",mode,"\n")
  K <- kurtosis(NPot)
  cat("Kurtosis : ",K,"\n")
  S <- skewness(NPot)
  cat("Skewness : ",S,"\n")
  cat("\n")
  cat("\n")
  
  # Summary if Potable variable
  cat(paste("Summary of ", col , " if Potable\n"))
  cat("\n")
  print(summary(Pot))
  V<- var(Pot)
  cat("Variance : ",V,"\n")
  Sd <- sd(Pot)
  cat("Standard deviation : ",Sd,"\n")
  Pot.table <- table(Pot)
  mode <- names(Pot.table)[which.max(Pot.table)]
  cat("Mode : ",mode,"\n")
  K <- kurtosis(Pot)
  cat("Kurtosis : ",K,"\n")
  S <- skewness(Pot)
  cat("Skewness : ",S,"\n")
  
}


```

# Multivariate analysis

Now we will use the multivariate analysis to better understand the link between variables.
First of all we plot all with the pair plot.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", fig.height = 0.35, fig.width = 7}
colors <- c("Not Potable" = "#E06D53", "Potable" = "#4682B4")

par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend(
  "center",
  legend = c("Non Potabile", "Potabile"),
  fill = c("#E06D53", "#4682B4"),
  horiz = TRUE,       
  bty = "n",          
  cex = 1.2,          
  pt.cex = 1.5        
)
```


```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
pairs(
      Water.clear[,cols],
      col = colors[Water.clear$Potability],
      pch = 19,                                          
      cex = 0.6,                                         
      main = "Pair Plot for Variables considering the potability with colors"
)

```

In general we can observe an ellipsoid distribution for each pair and on the border of it not potable variables. This means that a combination of high or low level of two variables is sufficient to underline a not potable water. 

```{r,echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

C <- cor(Water.clear[,cols])
C

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```

All variables are not heavily correlated, meaning no collinearity. This will not affect our analysis.
```{r,echo=FALSE,comment=""}
corrplot.mixed(C, upper="color", tl.col="black", tl.cex=0.46) 
```

Also this graph give us the evidence of no correlation: almost every pair of variables is colored white, indicating no correlation.

# Logistic Regression
First, we start our analysis doing the univariate case of the logistic regression, then we will go through the multivariate case.




## Univariate Logistic Regression

First we divide the dataset in Train and Test, respectively 70/30.
```{r,echo=FALSE,comment=""}
set.seed(1500)
alpha=0.7
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(Water.clear$Potability, p = alpha, 
                                  list = FALSE, 
                                  times = 1)
Water.L<-Water.clear[trainIndex,]
Water.T<-Water.clear[-trainIndex,]
nL <- nrow(Water.L)
nT <- nrow(Water.T)

```
After the split we train our model on the training set and see the result for each variable.
Then we do an analysis on polynomials of different grade up to 5 for each variable.
This step is done using the CV aprroach to choose the best model among all of them.
```{r,echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

contrasts(Water.L$Potability)

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```
We can notice that for our model Potable is the probability that the logistic function will predict.


### ph
```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
  fit.ph <- glm(Potability~ph, family = binomial, data = Water.L)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

print(summary(fit.ph, digits = 3))

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```


In this case $Pr(>|z|) > 0.05$ for $\beta_{1}$, then we cannot reject the hypothesis that $\beta_{1} = 0$. This means that there is no evidence that the potability depends \textbf{only} on that variable.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
cv.error.ph<-rep(0,5)
for(i in 1:5){
    poli.fit.ph <- glm(Potability~ poly(ph,i),family=binomial, data = Water.)
    cv.error.ph[i]<-cv.glm(Water.L,poli.fit.ph,K=10)$delta[1]
  }
```


```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
degree <- seq(1,5,1)
plot(degree,cv.error.ph, type="l", col="red",
       main="5-fold CV of ph",ylab = "CV error",)
```
There is no significant change in the CV error. All of this means that any polynomial until degree 5 does not affect significantly the result.



```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

glm.pred2.L.ph <- rep("Not Potable",nL)
glm.probs2.L.ph <- predict.glm(fit.ph,type="response")
glm.pred2.L.ph[glm.probs2.L.ph>.5]<-"Potable"
confMat2_L.ph<-addmargins(table(glm.pred2.L.ph,Water.L$Potability))
accuracy2_L.ph<-(confMat2_L.ph[1,1])/nL*100 
Err2_L.ph<-100-accuracy2_L.ph
  
cat("Confusion matrix for training set of ph")
print(confMat2_L.ph)
cat("Accuracy:",accuracy2_L.ph,"\n")
cat("Err:",Err2_L.ph,"\n")
cat("\n")
  
  

  
glm.pred2.T.ph <- rep("Not Potable",nT)
glm.probs2.T.ph <- predict.glm(fit.ph,type="response",newdata = Water.T)
glm.pred2.T.ph[glm.probs2.T.ph>.5]<-"Potable"
confMat2_T.ph<-addmargins(table(glm.pred2.T.ph,Water.T$Potability))
accuracy2_T.ph<-(confMat2_T.ph[1,1])/nT*100 
Err2_T.ph<-100-accuracy2_T.ph
  
cat("Confusion matrix for test set of ph")
print(confMat2_T.ph)
cat("Accuracy:",accuracy2_T.ph,"\n")
cat("Err:",Err2_T.ph,"\n")

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n")
```
The result confirm our hypothesis: the model cannot predict correctly our result. 


### Hardness

There is no significant change in the CV error. All of this means that any polynomial until degree 5 does not affect significantly the result.




## Multivariate Logistic regression

We want to estimate the best combination of predictors for our model(see Appendix B to how it's done). Also in this case we use the K-fold CV.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}

cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

n.train <- nrow(Water.L)
p <- length(cols)
k <- 10

folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length = n.train))

# We want to create a manual k-fold partition of the data
# this because if we use the function cv.glm every time in the main for loop
# this will generate at each step a different k-fold and it is not technically
# the better method. We want that all the combination are trained on the same
# k fold data
idx_0 <- which(Water.L$Potability == "Not Potable")
idx_1 <- which(Water.L$Potability == "Potable")

folds[idx_0] <- sample(rep(1:k, length = length(idx_0)))
folds[idx_1] <- sample(rep(1:k, length = length(idx_1)))


print(table(Fold = folds, Potability = Water.L$Potability))

all.models <- list()
for (size in 1:p) {
  # Create a matrix where each column is a combination 
  # of size "size" of predictors
  comb.mat <- combn(cols, size)
  
  # Cycle to create all the possible combination and save them
  # inside the list all models
  for (col.idx in 1:ncol(comb.mat)) {
    vars.subset <- comb.mat[, col.idx]
    all.models[[length(all.models) + 1]] <- list(
      size = size,
      vars = vars.subset,
      formula = as.formula(paste("Potability ~", paste(vars.subset, collapse = " + ")))
    )
  }
}

# A vector that is the same size of the number of models
cv.err.rates <- numeric(length(all.models))


for (m in seq_along(all.models)) {
  # Taking the formula
  form.m <- all.models[[m]]$formula
  # Creating a vector of the size of k-fold in our case 10
  fold.errs <- numeric(k)
  
  # Cycle for the k-fold
  for (j in 1:k) {
    tr.fold  <- Water.L[folds != j, ]
    val.fold <- Water.L[folds == j, ]
    
    # Doing the fit on the selected formula and on the trian set of the k-fold
    fit <- glm(form.m, data = tr.fold, family = binomial)
    
    # Deriving the probabilities
    probs <- predict(fit, newdata = val.fold, type = "response")
    
    # Renaiming the prediction 
    preds <- ifelse(probs > 0.5, "Potable", "Not Potable")
    
    # Defining the error rate for each k fold
    fold.errs[j] <- mean(preds != val.fold$Potability)
  }
  
  # Doing the mean of each k-fold to have a measure of the goodnes of that
  # possible cobination of predictors
  cv.err.rates[m] <- mean(fold.errs)
}

# Choosing the best index
best.idx <- which.min(cv.err.rates)
best.model <- all.models[[best.idx]]

cat(strrep("-", 70), "\n")
cat("Best model:\n")
print(best.model$formula)
cat("Number of predictors :", best.model$size, "\n")
cat("Predictors :", paste(best.model$vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("CV error:", round(cv.err.rates[best.idx], 4), "\n")
cat(strrep("-", 70), "\n")

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")

```
After choosing the best model on the training set, we will see the result on the test set.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

fit.final <- glm(best.model$formula, data = Water.L, family = binomial)
print(summary(fit.final))

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```
From this result we can understand that the logistic regression cannot explain the data: using this model the combination of our predictors is not sufficient in predicting some patterns. 

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

predicted.m <- rep("Not Potable",nT)
prediction.m <- predict.glm(fit.final,type="response",newdata = Water.T)
predicted.m[prediction.m>.5]<-"Potable"
confMat2_T.m<-addmargins(table(predicted.m,Water.T$Potability))
accuracy2_T.m<-(confMat2_T.m[1,1]+confMat2_T.m[2,2])/nT*100 
Err2_T.m<-100-accuracy2_T.m
  
cat("Confusion matrix for test set of Turbidity")
print(confMat2_T.m)
cat("Accuracy:",accuracy2_T.m,"\n")
cat("Err:",Err2_T.m,"\n")

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```
The Accuracy confirms our result: it's equal to the percentage of Not Potable water.

# QDA
Let's try the QDA for our analysis.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", results='asis'}

cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")

qda_all <- qda(Potability ~ ., data = Water.L)
pred_qda <- predict(qda_all, newdata = Water.T)$class
conf_qda <- addmargins(table(pred_qda,Water.T$Potability))
accuracy.qda<-(conf_qda[1,1]+conf_qda[2,2])/nT*100 
Err_qda <- 100 - accuracy.qda

print(conf_qda)
cat("Accuracy: ",accuracy.qda,"\n")
cat("Error rat: ",Err_qda)

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```
In this case the result is completely different. We can observe that only 56 Potable water samples are misclassified as not potable. We will analyze the ROC curve to evaluate the effect of changing the decision threshold trade-off.

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment=""}
pred_qda_ROC <- predict(qda_all, newdata = Water.T) 
prob_qda <- pred_qda_ROC$posterior[, "Potable"]
prediction.qda <- prediction(prob_qda, Water.T$Potability)
perf.qda <- performance(prediction.qda, measure = "tpr", x.measure = "fpr") 
plot(perf.qda,colorize=TRUE,lwd=2) 
plot(perf.qda,colorize=TRUE,lwd=2, print.cutoffs.at=c(0.2,0.5,0.8)) 
abline(a=0,b=1, lty=2)

qda.auc <- performance(prediction.qda, measure = "auc") 
cat("AUC: ",qda.auc@y.values[[1]])

```

Through our graph and AUC we can see a good prediction for our model.

The algorithm for pruning doesn't work.

# Conclusion
What is happening to our analysis? Why do almost all the algorithms fail? The answer lies in the intrinsic structure of our dataset. If we closely examine the univariate analysis, we can observe that for potable and not potable water have the same distribution for each class. This means that Logistic Regression cannot detect a clear threshold to split the data based on potability.

Furthermore, observing the multivariate analysis (pairs plot), the data exhibits a clear ellipsoidal distribution. The true decision boundary between the two classes is an ellipse. This means that a linear model, such as Logistic Regression and LDA, cannot capture this geometry and so cannot separate the data between the two classes. Only QDA works because it is based on non-linear relations that can capture the shape of our data.

Why didn't pruning work? This is likely due to the nature of our data. The reduction in the classification error rate is so small that the algorithm fails, causing the model to collapse to a single root node. Conversely, the three ensemble methods succeed because they bypass this structural limitation. We can see that these methods significantly improve the overall results, although they ultimately achieve very similar accuracy among themselves.

This analysis demonstrates that non-linear and ensemble models are strictly required to properly classify this dataset.


# Appendix A
Let's try a non linear logistic model. In our case only for demonstration we will use an equation associated to an ellipse with ph and Hardness as variables.
```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", error=TRUE, results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")
not.linear.fit <- glm(Potability ~ I(ph^2)+I(Hardness^2)+ph:Hardness+ph+Hardness,
                family = binomial, data = Water.L)
print(summary(not.linear.fit, digits = 3))

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")

```

```{r, echo=FALSE,comment="", error=TRUE, results='asis'}
cat("\\begin{lstlisting}\n")
non.linear.pred.L <- rep("Not Potable",nL)
non.linear.prob.L <- predict.glm(not.linear.fit,type="response")
non.linear.pred.L[non.linear.prob.L>.5]<-"Potable"
confMatNotL.L<-addmargins(table(non.linear.pred.L,Water.L$Potability))
accuracyNotL.L<-(confMatNotL.L[1,1]+confMatNotL.L[2,2])/nL*100 
ErrNotL.L<-100-accuracyNotL.L
  
cat("Confusion matrix for training set of Chloramines")
print(confMatNotL.L)
cat("Accuracy:",accuracyNotL.L,"\n")
cat("Err:",ErrNotL.L,"\n")
cat("\n")
  
  

non.linear.pred.T <- rep("Not Potable",nT)
non.linear.prob.T <- predict.glm(not.linear.fit,type="response",newdata = Water.T)
non.linear.pred.T[non.linear.prob.T>.5]<-"Potable"
confMatNotL.T<-addmargins(table(non.linear.pred.T,Water.T$Potability))
accuracyNotL.T<-(confMatNotL.T[1,1]+confMatNotL.T[2,2])/nT*100 
ErrNotL.T<-100-accuracyNotL.T
  
cat("Confusion matrix for test set of Chloramines")
print(confMatNotL.T)
cat("Accuracy:",accuracyNotL.T,"\n")
cat("Err:",ErrNotL.T,"\n")

cat("\\end{lstlisting}\n\n")
```
In this case we obtain a result, because we are using a non linear model that allows to recreate an appropriate shape for our data e separate them in a correct manner.

In our model we modify the accuracy's formula, this because the original formula in our code will be written as follow:
```{r}
accuracy2_T.ph<-(confMat2_T.ph[1,1]+confMat2_T.ph[2,2])/nT*100 
```
It takes the diagonal elements, but the second element is the sum, not the count of predicted against true Potable.
So I modified my formula like this:
```{r}
accuracy2_T.ph<-(confMat2_T.ph[1,1])/nT*100
```

This is done for every variable because all the variables have the same problem.

## Multivariate logistic regression


```{r, eval=FALSE}
n.train <- nrow(Water.L)
p <- length(cols)
k <- 10

folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length = n.train))

# We want to create a manual k-fold partition of the data
# this because if we use the function cv.glm every time in the main for loop
# this will generate at each step a different k-fold and it is not technically
# the better method. We want that all the combination are trained on the same
# k fold data
idx_0 <- which(Water.L$Potability == "Not Potable")
idx_1 <- which(Water.L$Potability == "Potable")

folds[idx_0] <- sample(rep(1:k, length = length(idx_0)))
folds[idx_1] <- sample(rep(1:k, length = length(idx_1)))


print(table(Fold = folds, Potability = Water.L$Potability))

all.models <- list()
for (size in 1:p) {
  # Create a matrix where each column is a combination 
  # of size "size" of predictors
  comb.mat <- combn(cols, size)
  
  # Cycle to create all the possible combination and save them
  # inside the list all models
  for (col.idx in 1:ncol(comb.mat)) {
    vars.subset <- comb.mat[, col.idx]
    all.models[[length(all.models) + 1]] <- list(
      size = size,
      vars = vars.subset,
      formula = as.formula(paste("Potability ~", paste(vars.subset, collapse = " + ")))
    )
  }
}

# A vector that is the same size of the number of models
cv.err.rates <- numeric(length(all.models))


for (m in seq_along(all.models)) {
  # Taking the formula
  form.m <- all.models[[m]]$formula
  # Creating a vector of the size of k-fold in our case 10
  fold.errs <- numeric(k)
  
  # Cycle for the k-fold
  for (j in 1:k) {
    tr.fold  <- Water.L[folds != j, ]
    val.fold <- Water.L[folds == j, ]
    
    # Doing the fit on the selected formula and on the trian set of the k-fold
    fit <- glm(form.m, data = tr.fold, family = binomial)
    
    # Deriving the probabilities
    probs <- predict(fit, newdata = val.fold, type = "response")
    
    # Renaiming the prediction 
    preds <- ifelse(probs > 0.5, "Potable", "Not Potable")
    
    # Defining the error rate for each k fold
    fold.errs[j] <- mean(preds != val.fold$Potability)
  }
  
  # Doing the mean of each k-fold to have a measure of the goodnes of that
  # possible cobination of predictors
  cv.err.rates[m] <- mean(fold.errs)
}

# Choosing the best index
best.idx <- which.min(cv.err.rates)
best.model <- all.models[[best.idx]]

cat(strrep("-", 70), "\n")
cat("Best model:\n")
print(best.model$formula)
cat("Number of predictors :", best.model$size, "\n")
cat("Predictors :", paste(best.model$vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("CV error:", round(cv.err.rates[best.idx], 4), "\n")
cat(strrep("-", 70), "\n")

```
